summary:
Snapshot 2026-10-07 21:20 UTC. Channel focus: plague. The Irkutsk story has gone from emerging to rising, close to peaking in mainstream news. It got about 70 Google News items in 48 hours (AP, NYT, BBC, NBC, CNN, Reuters, WaPo, Scientific American, The Conversation), and the Wikipedia article "Plague (disease)" got 32,054 views/day and is new in the top 1000. In our own snapshots, "Can pneumonic plague spread person to person?" has held at momentum 90+ across 2 snapshots.

Status as of Oct 7, 2026 (verified):
- **Russian authorities:** Rospotrebnadzor calls it "pneumonia of unknown etiology". It reports nearly 5,000 tests with no dangerous pathogens found and says there is "no epidemic risk". Russia told WHO it did not register any plague case in Irkutsk oblast.
- **WHO:** It has asked Russia for more details on the cause, the pathogen behind the public-health measures, and media reports of a second staff member with pneumonia of unclear origin. Russia called those second-case reports "false information".
- **WHO risk levels:** reported as "moderate to low" in the Irkutsk region, "low" for the rest of Russia and "very low" for Europe. Get the exact wording from the WHO source before publishing.
- **CDC:** Director Erica Schwartz (via Reuters) said the risk to the US from the unconfirmed case is extremely low. CDC is ready to monitor and screen arrivals from the region, including through its JFK port health station.
- **US State Department:** It has formally asked Russia for more information, and the US Embassy issued a health alert. The Moscow Times reports the embassy urged citizens to leave Russia, but that reflects the existing do-not-travel advisory, so confirm before citing.
- **Contacts:** about 197 identified, all reportedly without symptoms and testing negative (regional governor, Oct 2). Euronews reports over 90% have completed monitoring.
- **Unverified claims:** details such as a broken test tube come from unverified Ukrainian and Russian outlets. They are not official and must not be presented as fact.

What the opportunity looks like now:
- **The news itself is peaking.** Every major outlet has a "what is pneumonic plague" explainer, so generic explainers face high competition.
- **The best openings are specific search questions with "plague" as the subject that the news creates but doesn't fully answer.** That includes a dated status decoder (the second-case report, "no plague registered", WHO risk levels), why travel screening is happening, what preventive antibiotics for contacts means, and the live vaccine Russian lab staff receive. The playbook says rising-stage, plain-question titles perform best, so that is where we should aim.
- **Lab-safety and history angles are less covered and evidence-rich.** Examples are the 2009 US lab worker who died after infection with a weakened plague strain linked to an iron-overload condition (MMWR), and Madagascar 2017. They are low-competition and still get demand from the news hook.
- **Exclude:** bioweapon/Rand Paul "weaponized" framing, Trump–Putin political angles, cover-up narratives, the patient's name, and the CryptoRank "PLAGUE" token. All are rejected or excluded under our guardrails.

Every candidate below must carry a dated status line and the "if you're worried, talk to a health professional" line.

Sources: [Euronews](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/russia-dismisses-transparency-calls-amid-reports-of-second-siberia-plague-case), [Washington Times](https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/oct/7/who-seeks-clarity-russia-suspected-plague-death-possible-second-case/), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/06/world/russian-plague-outbreak-what-we-know-intl), [Reuters via TradingView](https://www.tradingview.com/news/reuters.com,2026:newsml_L4N45T1BB:0-cdc-sees-low-plague-risk-monitors-siberia-arrivals-after-worker-death-director-says/), [hromadske](https://hromadske.ua/en/world/272107-us-issues-health-alert-over-suspected-plague-case-in-russia-as-who-says-outbreak-risk-is-low), [Moscow Times](https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2026/10/07/us-embassy-urges-citizens-to-leave-russia-over-siberian-plague-suspicions-a93899), [Meduza](https://meduza.io/en/news/2026/10/02/hospital-in-russia-s-irkutsk-region-quarantined-amid-reports-that-a-patient-died-of-pneumonic-plague), [UNN](https://unn.ua/en/news/in-the-russian-federation-a-young-woman-died-of-plague-nearly-200-people-who-had-been-in-contact-with-her-were-hospitalized), [PMC live plague vaccine EV](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4317636), [CDC Yellow Book plague](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/yellowbook/2024/infections-diseases/plague), [HealthDay 2009 lab case](https://www.healthday.com/health-news/public-health/u-s-plague-fatality-isolated-lab-incident-new-report-confirms-654399.html).

candidates.topic: Irkutsk plague case status decoder: 'pneumonia of unknown etiology' vs 'suspected pneumonic plague', the reported second staff illness, and what WHO is asking Russia for (as of Oct 7, 2026)
candidates.angle: A calm 'confirmed / reported / unknown' three-column decoder. Russia told WHO it registered no plague case and reports nearly 5,000 negative tests. WHO is still asking about the cause and about media reports of a second staff member with pneumonia of unclear origin, which Russia calls false. Key line: not confirmed isn't the same as ruled out. Title: 'Irkutsk Plague Case: What's Confirmed vs Suspected (as of Oct 7)'.
candidates.why_now: WHO's request for clarification and the second-case reports broke on Oct 7, and today's news cycle is about mixed messages. People are searching for 'is it confirmed', and most coverage is political rather than a clean status breakdown. The decoder title formula is our best performer (150 long-form).

evidence.signal: Rospotrebnadzor: nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous pathogens and 'no epidemic risk'. WHO asked about 'a second staff member with pneumonia of unclear origin', and the Kremlin called the reports false. Over 90% of contacts have completed monitoring.
WHO asked about the cause, the pathogen behind the measures, and the second-case reports. Russia told WHO it registered no plague case in Irkutsk oblast.
UN health agency wants more details from Russia on suspected pneumonic plague case

candidates.topic: Can pneumonic plague spread person to person? Close-contact respiratory droplets, not measles-style airborne spread
candidates.angle: Answer in 10 seconds. CDC says pneumonic plague can spread person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact, and bubonic and septicemic plague don't spread that way. Then show how this differs from measles and COVID, and why it makes contact tracing work. Title: 'Can Pneumonic Plague Spread Person to Person?'
keywords: can pneumonic plague spread person to person
candidates.why_now: This is the top question in every explainer (BBC, NPR, CNN, WaPo). The Wikipedia page is getting 32k views/day, and it is the 3rd snapshot in a row at 90+ momentum. People want a direct yes/no answer, and the playbook's plain-question format fits it best.

evidence.signal: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
Plague (disease): 32,054 views/day, new in top 1000
Why a global outbreak of pneumonic plague is unlikely

candidates.topic: What the risk levels actually say: WHO 'moderate to low' in Irkutsk region, 'low' for the rest of Russia, 'very low' for Europe, plus CDC's 'extremely low' risk to the US
candidates.angle: 'How worried should you be?', answered only with what agencies have said, quoting each agency for its own region. Explain what a risk assessment weighs (transmission route, contacts, treatment availability). Title: 'Russia Plague Report: What WHO and CDC Say the Risk Is (as of Oct 7)'.
keywords: should i be worried about plague
is plague coming to the US
candidates.why_now: 'Should you be worried?' headlines are everywhere (Scientific American, TODAY, The Times, People). The CDC director's statement came out on Oct 7 via Reuters. Attributed-number formats land near our median.

evidence.signal: CDC Director Erica Schwartz: risk to the US from the unconfirmed case is extremely low, and CDC is ready to monitor and screen travelers
WHO risk: 'moderate to low' in Irkutsk region, 'low' for the rest of Russia, 'very low' for Europe. Check this against WHO's primary statement before publishing.
A suspected case of pneumonic plague is raising fears of an outbreak. Should you be worried?

candidates.topic: Why the CDC is screening travelers from Siberia: how port health stations and traveler monitoring work (JFK quarantine station)
candidates.angle: A brand-new, practical explainer of what 'monitoring arrivals' means: quarantine stations, symptom checks, and what a returning traveler with symptoms should do (contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and mention the travel). CDC's Yellow Book says no plague cases among US travelers returning in over 40 years. Title: 'Why Is the CDC Monitoring Travelers From Siberia?'
candidates.why_now: Axios ('U.S. tracking Siberia travelers') and Reuters both broke this on Oct 7. Almost no creator explainers exist yet, and it's a concrete action story for our US audience.

evidence.signal: U.S. tracking Siberia travelers after suspected plague case
CDC port health station at JFK can do surveillance and screening. CDC is working with DHS and State.
Risk to travelers is low. No plague cases reported among travelers returning to the US in more than 40 years.
How airlines could help contain Russian plague using lessons from past outbreaks

candidates.topic: Is plague curable? How antibiotics work against pneumonic plague, and why the first 24 hours matter
candidates.angle: Hopeful and factual. CDC says plague is treatable with common antibiotics, and pneumonic plague is fatal without treatment, so starting early is everything. No drug names with doses, and never self-treat: if you have possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Title: 'Is Plague Curable With Antibiotics?'
candidates.why_now: The death is driving 'can you survive it?' searches, and People, CNN and NPR explainers raise survivability without making it the headline. It's a reassuring counterweight that fits our tone.

evidence.signal: What is pneumonic plague and how dangerous is it?
Are We at Risk of Plague? An Expert Tackles Lingering Questions
What is pneumonic plague? (clinician explainer, Oct 7)

candidates.topic: Plague in the US: an average of 7 human cases a year (CDC), mostly in the rural West, plus pets, fleas and practical prevention
candidates.angle: 'The plague never went away' turned into practical, calm advice for US viewers: where it occurs (rural New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, California, Oregon, Nevada), how people get it (flea bites, handling sick animals, sick cats), and how to prevent it. Add the caveat that dog flea products can be toxic to cats. Title: 'CDC: Plague Still Occurs in the US. Here's Where and How to Avoid It'.
keywords: can you get plague from your cat
candidates.why_now: An AP piece ('The plague never went away… US nearly every year') was syndicated on Oct 7 to ABC, Boston Herald and others, so US readers are turning to local risk. It's evergreen with a fresh hook. Check the exact CDC average and range on the CDC page before publishing.

evidence.signal: The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year
Same AP story picked up by ABC, a sign of wide mainstream reach

candidates.topic: What happens to close contacts: about 197 people monitored, health authorities giving preventive antibiotics, and isolation. How contact tracing stops pneumonic plague
candidates.angle: An action explainer: 'Possible plague exposure? What health authorities do next.' Cover identifying contacts, the monitoring window, preventive antibiotics given by health authorities (never self-sourced) and isolation of anyone with symptoms. Use only attributed numbers: the regional governor reported contacts with no symptoms and negative tests (Oct 2), and Euronews reports over 90% have completed monitoring (Oct 7).
keywords: what happens if exposed to plague
candidates.why_now: The contact count and quarantine are the most concrete public-health facts in the story, and monitoring is near completion, which makes a natural 'what happens next' update point. The action-framed format performed well for us (57).

evidence.signal: 197 contacts identified. Governor Kobzev said on Oct 2 that contacts showed no signs of illness and tests were negative.
Over 90% of contacts completed medical monitoring
Russia says no plague found in contacts of Siberian lab worker who died

candidates.topic: The plague vaccine Russian lab staff get: the live EV vaccine used in former Soviet countries since the 1930s, and why there's no licensed plague vaccine for the general public in the US
candidates.angle: An under-covered explainer. Euronews reports the worker was vaccinated, and Russia's schedule vaccinates people who work with live plague cultures. Explain what the EV live vaccine is, what studies say about protection, why vaccines don't guarantee immunity, and why the US relies on antibiotics instead. Title: 'Is There a Plague Vaccine? What Lab Workers Get'.
keywords: can you get vaccinated against plague
candidates.why_now: 'She was vaccinated' raises an obvious question that almost no outlet has explained. There's a peer-reviewed review on EV vaccine history and little creator competition.

evidence.signal: Reports the worker was vaccinated against dangerous infections
Live EV vaccine has been used in former Soviet countries since the mid-1930s for at-risk groups, with evidence of protection against bubonic and pneumonic plague

candidates.topic: How labs that study plague keep it contained: BSL-3, protective gear and what happens after a lab exposure (Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, founded 1934)
candidates.angle: A behind-the-glass explainer: biosafety cabinets, respirators, directional airflow, vaccination of staff, and the post-exposure protocol (report, preventive antibiotics from occupational health, monitoring). Lab-accident details only as reported, attributed and hedged. Unverified broken-test-tube claims stay out. No bioweapon speculation.
candidates.why_now: Newsweek ('Everything We Know About Anti-Plague Lab') and Time ('What worries experts') put the lab at the centre of the story. It's the 3rd snapshot for this topic and still has few creator explainers.

evidence.signal: Everything We Know About Anti-Plague Lab At Center of Russia Outbreak Fears
What Worries Experts About the Russia 'Plague' Incident

candidates.topic: The last time plague killed a US lab worker: the 2009 Chicago case with a weakened strain and an iron-overload condition (CDC MMWR)
candidates.angle: A history precedent that gives perspective without fear. A researcher died after working with an attenuated Y. pestis strain, and the investigation linked it to undiagnosed hereditary haemochromatosis. CDC called it an isolated lab incident, and no contacts got sick. Shows how lab exposures are investigated. Title: 'Has Plague Killed a Lab Worker Before? What the 2009 US Case Taught Us'.
candidates.why_now: The news hook naturally raises 'has this happened before?'. Almost no current coverage revisits the CDC-documented US precedent, so competition is very low and the source is primary (MMWR 2011).

evidence.signal: U.S. plague fatality an 'isolated' lab incident, report confirms. Weakened strain, iron overload condition.
Plague kills U.S. lab worker

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague symptoms and timing: fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, typically 1–4 days after exposure (CDC), and when to get urgent care
candidates.angle: A symptom card using CDC's full pneumonic warning signs and incubation wording (check the exact CDC page at publish time). Make clear these symptoms matter only with possible exposure, because ordinary flu season is starting. Close: contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
keywords: how long does plague take to show symptoms
candidates.why_now: Newsweek ran a 'symptoms explained' piece and NPR, Nevada Public Radio and the Sacramento Bee all have explainers. Symptom questions overlap with the start of flu season, so we can add value by framing them around exposure context.

evidence.signal: Pneumonic plague symptoms explained after Russian scientist's death
What is the pneumonic plague?

candidates.topic: Pneumonic vs bubonic vs septicemic plague: three forms of Yersinia pestis, and why only pneumonic passes between people
candidates.angle: A clear 3-panel comparison naming all three forms. Cover entry route, typical signs, and person-to-person spread, keeping CDC's hedges ('can spread' for pneumonic; bubonic can progress to the lungs). Title: 'Pneumonic vs Bubonic Plague: What's the Difference?'
candidates.why_now: Wikipedia demand is spiking and BusinessToday-style 'pneumonic or bubonic' pieces are trending. This is the 3rd snapshot for the topic, and it gives evergreen search value beyond the news cycle.

evidence.signal: Plague (disease) at 32,054 views/day
Russia plague outbreak scare: pneumonic or bubonic, key differences

candidates.topic: Madagascar 2017: how a large pneumonic plague outbreak was stopped with contact tracing and preventive antibiotics
candidates.angle: A real-world proof that modern public health stops pneumonic plague: urban pneumonic spread, then mass contact tracing, preventive antibiotics given by health authorities, and treatment centres. Use WHO's published totals, checked at the WHO source. Title: 'How Madagascar Stopped Pneumonic Plague in 2017'.
candidates.why_now: Experts in The Conversation and BBC cite past outbreaks to explain why global spread is unlikely. Few creators tell the Madagascar story in depth, and it gives a calm, evidence-led long-form option.

evidence.signal: An expert explains what we know so far and why there's no need to panic
Why a global outbreak of pneumonic plague is unlikely

candidates.topic: Black Death (1300s) vs plague in 2026: same bacterium, but antibiotics, diagnostics and public health change the picture
candidates.angle: Name both sides: what was the same (Y. pestis, fleas, rodents) and what changed (antibiotics since the 1940s, rapid tests, contact tracing). Never frame it as a 'new Black Death'. Title: 'Black Death vs Today: What Antibiotics Changed'.
keywords: could the black death happen again
candidates.why_now: Smithsonian and Popular Mechanics are invoking the 'disease behind the Black Death', and doom-framed coverage exists, so a calm, factual comparison stands out.

evidence.signal: Lab death sparks concerns over the disease behind the Black Death: here's what to know

candidates.topic: Plague myths already circulating, corrected: 'airborne like COVID', 'no cure', 'you can catch it from someone with bubonic plague'
candidates.angle: Attributed myth corrections, each naming the agency. Correct beliefs people already hold without amplifying bioweapon or cover-up rumours. Not proven is not the same as a myth, so keep the hedges. Title: 'Is Plague Airborne Like COVID? 3 Plague Myths Checked'.
keywords: is there a cure for plague
candidates.why_now: Russia is warning about 'false information' and US outlets are running fear-heavy headlines (Popular Mechanics 'Terrified'). Misconceptions are spreading on social media faster than corrections.

evidence.signal: Russia warns against spreading 'false information' as reports emerge of second plague case
Top 8 questions about the 'plague' situation

candidates.topic: US Embassy health alert and travel advisory for Russia over the suspected plague case: what it actually says
candidates.angle: Cut through the headlines. The embassy alert cites press reports and quarantine measures in Irkutsk, and the 'urge to leave' wording reflects Russia's existing do-not-travel level. Confirm the exact text at the State Department source before publishing. Separate the travel advisory from health risk (CDC: extremely low risk to the US). Political framing is out.
candidates.why_now: Moscow Times, The Hill, Newsweek and the Daily Beast are running conflicting headlines ('urges citizens to leave', 'drops urgent warning'). There's a narrow window for a clear correction, but the story is politically charged and fast-moving.

evidence.signal: U.S. Embassy urges citizens to leave Russia over Siberian plague suspicions
State Department reissues do-not-travel warning amid suspected pneumonic plague
Trump admin drops urgent plague warning (conflicting coverage)

candidates.topic: 'Russian plague is a bioweapon' / 'weaponized' claims (Rand Paul, Trump 'we hope not')
candidates.angle: Do not cover. It breaks our no-bioweapon-speculation guardrail and is misinformation bait. If myths content touches it, say only that health agencies are treating this as a public-health investigation, and don't repeat the claim.
candidates.why_now: High political news volume, but outside our guardrails.

Trump says US doesn't believe Russian plague is a bioweapon
